Yes, that's exactly it, and your fix is the right one. Here's the mechanism behind the silence: a list iterator is nothing but a stored integer index plus a reference to the list. Each `next()` hands back element[i] and increments i. When you delete an element at or before position i, everything after it slides one slot to the left, but the iterator's counter keeps marching forward — so the element that just slid into the vacated slot is stepped straight over. That's why 'a' got removed and 'of' was still seen (it slid into index 0, and the iterator had already moved to index 1, which by then held 'of'), while 'in' slid into a position the counter had already passed. The loop also terminates early rather than raising, because the iterator just stops once i reaches the now-shorter length; dicts and sets can afford to raise RuntimeError because they carry a modification counter, while lists deliberately don't pay for one. Iterating over a snapshot is perfectly idiomatic and the standard cure. Two things worth knowing about it: `remove` searches from the front, so if the list contains duplicates you'll delete the first match rather than the one you're looking at, and each `remove` is O(n), making the whole thing quadratic. For a pure filter like this, most Python programmers would skip the mutation entirely and build a fresh list with a comprehension, which is linear and sidesteps the whole question. If the caller genuinely needs the original list object updated in place, assigning that comprehension back into `words[:]` gives you in-place semantics without any iteration hazard.

    index = {}
    for emp in employees:
        dept = emp["dept"]
        index.get(dept, []).append(emp["name"])
    return index

    {"name": "Ana", "dept": "eng"},
    {"name": "Boris", "dept": "ops"},
    {"name": "Chen", "dept": "eng"},
]

```

Ugh, of course. Nothing holds a reference — the default list I hand to `get` is just a temporary; `get` reads the dict, it never writes to it, so I was appending into an object that got dropped on the next line. I swapped the line for `index.setdefault(dept, []).append(emp["name"])` and now I get `{'eng': ['Ana', 'Chen'], 'ops': ['Boris']}` exactly as expected.

That's exactly it, and your diagnosis is precisely right. The read-only nature of that lookup was the whole story: when the key is absent it constructs your default, hands it back, and leaves the dictionary untouched — so `['Ana']` was a perfectly real list that simply had no owner once the statement ended and was collected immediately. That also explains why you saw no error: appending to a list always works, whether or not anyone is watching. The accessor you moved to differs in exactly one respect that matters here — on a miss it inserts the default under the key before returning it, so the object you mutate is the same object the dictionary now holds, and every later hit on that key returns that same list and accumulates into it. Worth noting the identity subtlety too: because the default is evaluated eagerly, you build a fresh empty list on every iteration even when the key already exists; it's harmless, just discarded. If that allocation ever shows up in a profile, or if you want the accumulate-on-miss behaviour to be the container's job rather than the call site's, `collections.defaultdict(list)` gives you the same semantics with the default constructed lazily. Nice work tracking it down from the reference angle rather than guessing at the data.

def parse_log(path):
    with open(path) as f:
        for line in f:
            parts = line.strip().split("|")
            if len(parts) == 3:
                yield float(parts[1]), parts[2]

def report(path):
    entries = parse_log(path)
    peak = max(lat for lat, _ in entries)
    slow = [msg for lat, msg in entries if lat > 0.9 * peak]
    return peak, slow
```

This is driving me slightly nuts. `report()` returns a sensible peak latency — 4.13 for my sample file, which matches what I get from grepping the log by hand — but `slow` always comes back as `[]`. I've checked the threshold arithmetic in a REPL and `0.9 * 4.13` is obviously below several of the latencies in the file, so the comparison isn't the problem. Good, so the records exist and the predicate is sound. Before the list comprehension runs its first comparison, how many items are still left to pull out of `entries`?

Ah — that landed. `entries` is a single generator object, and `max` drained it, so by the time the comprehension starts iterating there's nothing left and it just quietly builds an empty list instead of erroring. I changed the binding so `entries` is `list(parse_log(path))` and now both the peak and the slow list come out right. Slightly annoyed it failed silently rather than blowing up, but at least it makes sense now.

That's exactly right, and your diagnosis is the correct one. A generator object is an iterator, and an iterator's contract is one-way: each `__next__` call permanently advances its internal state, and once the frame returns it stays finished forever. `max` has to see every element to do its job, so it pulls until it gets `StopIteration` — and that's the crux of the silent failure you're annoyed about. Re-iterating an exhausted iterator isn't an error condition in Python; the very first `__next__` raises `StopIteration` again, which the `for` machinery inside your comprehension interprets as "the sequence is over," so you get a well-formed empty list rather than an exception. This is why a list or tuple behaves differently: those are iterables, not iterators, and each `for` over them asks for a brand-new iterator via `__iter__`, which is what makes multiple passes work. Binding the materialized records is the right call here, and it's worth knowing the alternatives for when it isn't: you can call `parse_log(path)` a second time to get a fresh generator and pay for a second disk pass, or restructure into a single pass that tracks the max and buffers candidates as it goes — useful if the log is too big to hold in memory. `itertools.tee` exists too, but it buffers everything the lagging consumer hasn't reached yet, so with `max` racing to the end it would cost you about the same memory as your list for no benefit. As a general smell: any time a generator is bound to a name and that name appears in more than one consuming expression, ask whether the second consumer will find anything left.

That's the fix, and your explanation of why is exactly right. Python walks the except clauses in source order and runs the first one whose class matches the raised exception, where "matches" means the exception is an instance of that class — subclasses included. The key mechanism is that scope in Python is decided at compile time, not line by line: if a name is bound anywhere in a function — by assignment, by a `for` target, or by being a parameter — the compiler marks it local for the entire body, and every lookup of that name inside the function goes straight to the local slot. It never falls back to builtins just because the local happens to hold something uncallable. So both of your failures were the same defect wearing two costumes. With no argument the local held None, hence 'NoneType' object is not callable. With an argument it held your one-parameter callback, and the call site handed it a function and an iterable because that's the signature of the builtin you thought you were invoking, hence 'takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given' pointing at a lambda that was indeed yours, just being invoked by machinery you never intended. That's also why the traceback felt so disorienting: the frame that raised was your lambda, but the caller was the tail line, not the loop. This trap is much nastier for parameters than for module-level assignments, because a module-level rebinding at least only affects lookups that happen after it runs, whereas a parameter poisons the name from the first line of the function. It's worth knowing that `filter`, `list`, `type`, `id`, `input`, `format`, and `next` are the usual casualties, since they read so naturally as argument names; flake8-builtins (the A002 check) or a Ruff rule will flag exactly this if you want a mechanical guard. Yes — that's the fix, and your explanation of it is right on the money. The defect was never in the cache or the data; it was that your function had two different timing contracts. The database branch necessarily emits from inside an asynchronous callback, so by the time any event fires, `streamReport` has long since returned and the caller's `.on('row', ...)` and `.on('end', ...)` are installed. The cached branch, though, ran the whole replay while the caller was still evaluating the expression `streamReport(42)` — the emitter existed, but nobody outside the function had a reference to it yet, so every `emit` went to zero listeners and was dropped on the floor. EventEmitter has no buffering, unlike a promise, so an event with no subscriber isn't queued for later; it's simply gone. That's why `listenerCount('row')` being 0 was the whole story in one number. This is the failure mode Node folks call "releasing Zalgo": an API that is sometimes synchronous and sometimes asynchronous is much worse than one that is consistently either, because callers can't write code that is correct in both cases. By deferring the replay you made the fast path obey the same contract as the slow one, and the caller no longer has to know or care whether the report was cached. Two things worth keeping in your pocket: if you ever want an ordering guarantee against I/O callbacks rather than just "after this function returns," the choice between the microtask-style and macrotask-style deferral helpers matters, and if you later want the emitter to be forgiving about late subscribers, the usual move is to switch to a pull-based abstraction — a stream or an async iterator — which buffers instead of discarding. To fill in the mechanics: when the engine enters `checkout` it creates bindings for every `var` in the function body up front and initializes each one to `undefined`. Only the *binding* is hoisted; the initializer on the right-hand side is an ordinary runtime statement that executes when control actually reaches that line. So at the moment your log ran, the name existed but held `undefined`, and `undefined(...)` is what produced "is not a function" rather than a ReferenceError about an unknown name — which is why the error message was misleadingly reassuring about the name being visible. Your instinct about the alternative is also right: a function declaration is hoisted whole, name and body together, so it's callable anywhere in the enclosing scope regardless of where you wrote it — that's the real behavioral difference between a declaration and a function expression stored in a variable, not just style. Worth knowing too that `let` and `const` behave differently again: the binding is created but left uninitialized in the temporal dead zone, so touching it early throws a ReferenceError that names the variable. That failure is noisier and usually easier to diagnose than the silent `undefined` you just chased, which is one practical argument for reaching for `const` over `var` for this kind of local helper.

RESISTANCE = [1000.0, 1210.0, 1480.0, 1820.0, 2250.0, 2790.0]

def resistance_at(temp_c):
    i = bisect.bisect_left(TEMP_C, temp_c)
    if i == 0:
        return RESISTANCE[0]
    if i >= len(TEMP_C):
        return RESISTANCE[-1]
    lo, hi = TEMP_C[i - 1], TEMP_C[i]

    return RESISTANCE[i - 1] + frac * (RESISTANCE[i] - RESISTANCE[i - 1])

That's exactly right, and it wasn't luck — you found the real defect. The rule that makes it work is that a `.then` callback's return value becomes the resolution value of the promise that `.then` produced, and if the callback returns nothing, that promise resolves with `undefined` right away. That's what was happening: the inner request was fired off, the callback fell off the end with no value, and the outer chain resolved immediately with `undefined`, which is why your final `.then` ran before the orders had arrived and blew up on the property access. The special case you've now taken advantage of is that when a `.then` callback hands back a promise instead of a plain value, the outer chain *adopts* it — it waits for that promise to settle and takes its value as its own. So the orders chain is now spliced into the main chain rather than dangling beside it. Two bonuses worth knowing: because the inner chain is part of the main chain now, a rejection in the orders request will also propagate to any `.catch` you attach at the end, whereas before it would have been an unhandled rejection nobody could see. And this whole class of mistake is much harder to make with `async`/`await`, since forgetting to wait is visible as a missing `await` right at the call site rather than as a missing keyword buried in a nested callback.

Comparison with == is a negotiated protocol: Python offers the left operand's __eq__ first, and only falls back to the right operand's reflected __eq__ if the left one returns NotImplemented. Your marker's inherited equality is identity-based, so the pattern *looks* like it works — but it only works when the other operand is well-behaved enough to decline or to answer with a plain bool. numpy deliberately does neither: it answers with an element-wise array, and a truth test on that is ambiguous by design. MagicMock is the other classic offender, answering truthy to almost anything, which is why that override was being read as absent. Pandas objects, ORM column proxies, and anything implementing a DSL-ish __eq__ will bite you the same way.
